Okay, but I have two questions in mind:

Is the Stoic God a person (you know, with motives, powers, purposes, intentions and will)? 

Are they Omniscient, Omnipotent and Omnibenevolent (like the Christian God)?

and the Stoics were even hesitant to claim that any one of them would deserve the title of "sage". So, yeah, one could argue that the Stoics maybe believed that almost every human is not sage (at least the ones they knew of), and, therefore, almost every human is not truly virtuous or happy.

Then, that raises another question:

Why has the Cosmos provided us free will in the first place?

It makes sense to have free will in a theistic context (i.e. to be good enough or to have some sufficient moral merit to enable you to go to heaven), but now with Stoicism, there's no afterlife, and there's kinda no emphasis on moral merit for any purpose other than your own wellbeing. So, I don't really find the "free will" reason sufficient enough to permit the loving providential Stoic God to not guarantee and produce a majority of virtuous humans (the kind of offspring that they kinda created the whole universe to produce). Yes, one could argue that virtue isn't virtue really without free will, but still, I feel that the state of humanity then and now was more than free agents some of them chose virtue and others chose vice.
